newsitem.title: USA: Soybeans collapse, gold prices steady, oil firm.
newsitem.headline: Soybeans collapse, gold prices steady, oil firm.

text.p: Soybean prices collapsed on Tuesday on market talk that imports from Brazil will alleviate tight supplies in the United States before an expected record soybean crop is harvested in the Midwest this fall.

In other markets, gold prices held above four-year lows in nervous trading and platinum group metals were steady on a lack of fresh news about renewed Russian sales. Oil prices rose on continued talk of delays in new Iraqi oil sales.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for July delivery plummeted 39 cents a bushel to close at $7.32.
The latest tumble in prices came one day after the market dropped sharply following an Agriculture Department estimate that farmers this year have planted the most soybeans since 1982.
Red-hot processor demand for soybeans, which yield useful products including industrial oils and animal feeds, had pushed soybean prices to 8-1/2 year highs of $9.03 in May.

Since then, prices have turned around on improved growing weather in the Midwest and confirmation that some major processors such as Minneapolis-based Cargill Inc. were importing soybeans from Brazil to keep plants supplied this summer.
"The purported squeeze in the July was thwarted," said John Kleist, grain analyst with Sagamore Partners.

"What stopped it was the realization that you can increase supplies by switching old crop sales to new crop, by canceling old crop sales, by getting early (harvested) beans out of the South, and by importing beans from Brazil," Kleist said.

The heavy selling in soybeans helped push down corn prices, with July corn ending down 4-3/4 cents a bushel at $2.43-1/4. July wheat closed 1-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $3.22-1/2, under pressure from newly arriving winter wheat supplies as harvest gets under way in the upper Midwest.
In New York, gold prices tested new four-year lows but platinum group metals ended little changed.
Gold for August delivery at the COMEX ended down 20 cents at $335.10 an ounce, holding above the life-of-contract low at $334.60 set on Monday.

The most recent slide in gold has been led by professional speculators, while investors have been driven away from precious metals by a strong U.S. stock market and dollar and U.S. consumer price inflation at 10-year lows.
"The outlook for both gold and silver still looks bearish, though we saw a little consolidation today," said John Tyree, a trader with broker FIMAT in New York.
September silver ended up 3.0 cents at $4.678 an ounce.
Platinum for October delivery at the New York Mercantile Exchange ended down 90 cents at $411.90 an ounce, while NYMEX September palladium closed up $1.40 at $176.30.

Russian officials had indicated that Russian exports of platinum group metals would resume in late June, but Russian spot market sales have not been reported and no cash metal deliveries have been reported, traders said.

Russia supplies about 60 percent of the world's palladium and 20 percent of its platinum, but exports have been suspended since December 1996, pushing spot prices and forward rates sharply higher this year.

"Do not sell short platinum or palladium," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said in a report. "Consumers, on the other hand, will just have to grin and bear it and continue to live on a hand-to-mouth basis and take prices as they come."
Oil prices rose, fueled by an expected decline in petroleum inventories and delays in Iraqi oil sales.
Crude oil for August delivery closed 32 cents higher at $20.12 a barrel, with August gasoline closing up 0.66 cent a gallon at 58.78 cents and August heating oil up 0.99 cent a gallon at 54.84 cents.
"There was short-covering as the market continues to focus on delays in Iraqi crude sales," said analyst Thomas Blakeslee at Cargill Investor Services in New York.
Iraqi diplomat Abdul Amir al-Anbari said over the weekend that he expected oil sales would resume in August. Many traders had expected Iraqi oil to enter the market again in July.

The United Nations has eased sanctions against Iraq and allowed it to sell oil in six-month periods on a renewable basis. Iraq was to start its second six months of sales on June 8, but fresh deals have been held up as details of Iraq's plans to distribute humanitarian aid were reviewed.
